root_cause_label: Preprocessing Boundary Collapse and Missing Mandatory Tokens (One-Sentence Corpus + Required Words Not Enforced)
one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent repeatedly wrote preprocess_text with re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text) before split('\n'), collapsing the entire corpus into one sentence, and simultaneously never enforced hard inclusion of required analogy words in the vocabulary, causing both structural training degradation and spec-violating missing tokens.
t_err_evidence: Step 8 appends preprocess_text with 'text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)' before 'text.split("\n")', collapsing all newline boundaries into spaces so the subsequent split yields essentially one long sentence; this is the first introduction of the decisive preprocessing bug.
t_commit_evidence: Step 29 rewrites preprocess_text a third time (after rm+rewrite cycles at steps 17-18 and 25) with the same newline-collapsing logic unchanged; no subsequent step ever touches preprocessing or fixes it before the final training run at step 36, locking in the failure.
t_surface_evidence: Step 36 training output explicitly prints 'Loaded 1 sentences' (corpus collapsed to one line) and 'Warning: Missing required words: {\'america\', \'daughter\', \'brother\'}', directly confirming both bugs.
trigger_explanation: The agent's code generation consistently reproduced the same preprocessing logic (collapsing \s+ before splitting on \n) across three independent rewrites of the file, even when explicitly warned in internal analysis annotations. It also generated vocabulary logic that conditionally adds required words only if present in word_counts rather than forcibly unioning them, demonstrating a persistent failure in generating correct implementation details for these two constraints.
forewarning_evidence: Step 16: SyntaxError on 'text.split(\'' (unterminated string literal at line 90), indicating file corruption; Step 23: same SyntaxError again after the first rewrite attempt, flagging repeated write-cycle failures before the decisive rewrite at step 29.
